tables.title: D1 by acquisition source: effect size and confidence
tables.note: Relative Δ is the effect size (use it for 'is this composition'); the paired t and the binomial z are confidence (use them for 'did it move at all'). A paired t beyond about ±2.8 is what 4 degrees of freedom need for 95%. The binomial floor only counts sampling noise inside a day, so it is always the stricter of the two. `Friends` arrive by invite and never see a thumbnail; `Search` looked the game up by name. The binomial floor assumes the D1 cohort is that source's new users.
tables.source: `splits.d1BySource` in `data/seal.json`; paired t = mean of the 5 same-weekday differences ÷ (their sd ÷ √5); new users = `UniqueUsersWithPlaySessions` by `AcquisitionSource`, filter `IsNewUser = New`, from `series.json`.

tables.title: How consistent is each rate move across the five weekday pairs?

tables.title: Seal against the other four games, day by day from 08 Sep
tables.note: 1.00 = this game moved exactly like the rest of the portfolio that day; below 1 = worse, above 1 = better (for crash rate, above 1 = more crashes). Each game is first divided by its own 01–07 Sep mean, so shared calendar or platform effects — the 08 Sep payer step, the Labor Day weekend — cancel. Rates are the reliable rows; for DAU and impressions the peers mix growing and decaying games, so read those rows as 'moved differently from the portfolio', not as a counterfactual.
tables.source: `run` series in reports/2026-09-19/data/<slug>.json (settled ONE_DAY headline). Index = (this game ÷ its own 01–07 Sep mean) ÷ median over the other four games of the same ratio. tools/r0919/peer-index.js
